I am 43 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou County for twenty years. My household has five people, and with some family members working off-farm, I manage most of the farm work myself. My 3 mu plot is devoted entirely to stevia. Over the years I have learned that stevia gives steady income because the buyers come to our village, and with only 3 mu I cannot afford to spread myself across many different crops.

It is spring now, so I will start by rotary tilling the soil to make a fine, loose seedbed. I will buy improved stevia seedlings from the county seedling station — I have tried saving my own cuttings before, but the bought seedlings grow more uniformly and the stevioside content is higher, which means better prices. Before transplanting in late April, I will spread farmyard manure across the field and work in compound fertilizer. Stevia needs nitrogen for leaf growth, so I will top-dress with urea after each cut to push new leaves. I have a well for irrigation, which is essential on the North China Plain, and I will water five times this season: immediately after transplanting, twice during the hot summer months, and twice after cutting to help the plants recover. I do not like using too many chemicals, but I will keep two pesticide applications ready — mainly for aphids that appear when the weather turns dry in July. I plan to harvest twice: once in mid-July and again in mid-October before the first frost. If the weather holds and I manage the water well, I expect to dry and collect about 400 kg of leaves per mu this year.
